intuition: Choosing one value from every list in all combinations quickly becomes impractical. A more useful candidate keeps one current representative per sorted list. The minimum and maximum of those representatives define a range that already covers every list.

To improve this range, advance the list that supplies its minimum. Advancing another representative cannot raise the lower endpoint and cannot reduce the upper endpoint, so it cannot produce a better range before the current minimum changes. A min heap locates the next list to advance, while a separate high value tracks the largest representative.

Each popped minimum yields a valid candidate before its list advances. Compare candidates by width first and left endpoint second, since equal-width ties must favor the earlier range. Sorted lists mean replacement values never move backward, so high only needs to increase. If the minimum’s list has no successor, stop: proceeding would drop that list’s coverage, and no later covering selection is possible. The heap remains one entry per list throughout the search.

steps: For the three example lists, representatives [4,0,5] produce initial range [0,5].
Advance the list supplying 0 to 9; then advance the list supplying 4 to 10.
Continue advancing only the smallest representative, exposing 18,12,15,20,24,22 in sequence.
Eventually the representatives are 24 from list 0, 20 from list 1, and 22 from list 2.
Their range [20,24] has width 4, improving the earlier width-5 best.
Popping 20 exhausts list 1, so stop and return [20,24].

codeNotes.note: The minimum identifies both the current range’s lower endpoint and the only list worth advancing.
Tuple ordering encodes the required width priority and smaller-left-endpoint tie-breaker.
An exhausted list prevents any later selection from retaining coverage of all lists.
